title: Splitting Data Across Machines
description: Learn the three main partitioning strategies — range-based, hash-based, and directory-based — plus how to handle hotspots and cross-partition queries.

segments.text: Your database has grown to a terabyte. One machine is groaning under the load. The answer? Split the data across multiple machines. This is partitioning, also called sharding. Let's learn to do it right.

Partitioning serves two goals: spreading data so no single machine runs out of space, and spreading load so no single machine is overwhelmed with queries. It's like splitting a library's books across multiple buildings by subject.

Range-based partitioning assigns contiguous key ranges to each partition. Users A through G on shard one, H through N on shard two, and so on. It's intuitive, and range queries are efficient — just ask the right shard.
But range-based has a dangerous flaw: hotspots. If most of your users' last names start with S, that shard gets hammered while others sit idle. Uneven data distribution leads to uneven load.

Hash-based partitioning fixes this. Hash the key, then assign to a partition based on the hash value. A good hash function scatters keys uniformly, so even clustered keys like 'Smith' and 'Stevens' land on different shards.
But hashing destroys key ordering. Want all users whose names start with 'S'? With range partitioning, it's one shard. With hash partitioning, you must query every shard and merge results.
segments.thought_prompt: When would you choose range-based over hash-based partitioning? Think about your query patterns.

segments.text: Directory-based partitioning uses a lookup table — a separate service that knows which partition holds each key. Maximum flexibility: you can move data around without changing the partitioning logic. The directory is the map.

The downside? That directory becomes a single point of failure and a potential bottleneck. Every data access must first consult the directory. If it goes down, nobody can find anything. You've traded one problem for another.

Even with hash partitioning, hotspots can appear. If one key is wildly popular — a celebrity's profile, a viral post — its partition gets crushed. Solutions include splitting hot keys across sub-partitions or adding a random suffix to distribute the load.

Cross-partition queries are the tax you pay for sharding. A query that spans multiple partitions must be sent to each one, results collected and merged. This scatter-gather pattern adds latency and complexity. It's often the biggest pain of sharded systems.

The choice of partition key determines everything. Pick wrong, and you get hotspots, expensive cross-partition joins, and unbalanced shards. Pick right, and sharding is almost invisible to the application.
segments.thought_prompt: For an e-commerce database, would you partition by user_id, order_id, or product_id? Why?

segments.text: Range partitioning keeps ordering but risks hotspots. Hash partitioning distributes evenly but loses ordering. Directory partitioning is flexible but adds a dependency. The art of sharding is choosing the strategy and partition key that match your access patterns.
